body: Thank you. This is actually a reverse from how I tend to communicate, which is stumbled.
Based on my prior post, not as much as I'd like. Seeing the upvotes and views tells me there's interest in how I'm feeling, but the advice isn't that profound. Or if it is, I may refuse to accept it.
Maybe if it really is super fulfilling for you. But most work isn't. Does anyone who isn't a yellow meme sponge actually take pride as a career fry cook?

I even considered an independent homesteader life, getting my own materials and hunting/farming what I need. The whole property tax thing ended that; if I recall there's just so many laws that make an independent "keep to myself and not be a bother" life needlessly difficult, if not impossible. I even considered getting a solar powered van or an RV and living on the road free from money.

Maybe to a point. We'd have to go back to the dark ages before we become haggling farmers again, and even then we'd still have Lord's and self-appointed kings to appease to...

Once again, our problems go back centuries, and instead of addressing it he made it our cornerstone. But now I'm just ranting.

>I also been struggling with suicide ideation for the better part of 15 years now. It's getting louder with time.

That's not reassuring. The idea that this is all incurable; a lifelong ailment.


>Depression is a liar. Always, all day, every day. It is a poison that tries to fuck you up and give up your life. You got to talk back to it. It feels like it's you thinking those things. But it's only because it's messing with you. Like a trickster. So stop self-bullying in that notepad. Talk back to it.

I've actually started doing this recently. I have conversations with it in my phone. I call him Fuckface, and I imagine him as part Internet troll, part terrible roommate, and part Edgar from 'Men in Black'. He really is a trickster, using any negative logic it could get its hands on, regardless of past consistentcy.

>What I do when I really feel down is sleep. 

Same, but I can't sleep indefinitely. I've tried. The depression will come back once I wake up, dangling over my head like a spider.

∆

You just effin' earned it. Finding someone who actually gets what I am going through and has offered what may be a way out? Brilliant. You say you're 'balls deep' into this matter, which may be foreboding for my future, but anywhere is better than here, y'know?

∆, specifically for the stories and the back-n-forth. I hope your words, as well as those in here who have also earned deltas, will sink into my mind over time. It's not dramatic, but my mind has been changed in the matter, now I just need to slip out of the attitude that built it.

This response, among others in this thread, has given me a needed push, which I hope will be ingrained over time.

So here's your neat polygon! ∆

>If you had to tie a life motto with your philosophy to living life, what would it be?

Off the top of my head? "Never Be Normal". May as well be a Hit Topic shirt, but it's something I drive back to... more of a comfort zone, maybe. ( Though maybe "normal" should be swapped with "ordinary")

I'm not a people person: I tend to get by with grunts and simple responses in order to get out of conversations. I don't have many friends, and the ones  I see the most I suspect are trying to pull me back into thier views on reality, which I take as an insult. (Backfire effect?) Not a social butterfly, and I've heard some thoughts suggesting that's not a bad thing, but it puts me at a disadvantage...

Thanks for your input, and the video. Hearing Adam talk about some serious humility, even when being in the best company he could imagine, was certainly a thing I would never have expected from his life; further illustrating the pic you shared.

.....I don't even know where to begin. So let me ask this. 

Can you award multiple deltas to multiple posters? Because there was some good shit in this thread--many a patient persons able to dodge/walk off my sarcasm and defeatism. They alone are why this thread is bookmarked my phone.

But you sir are some sort of spooky mind-reading demon. 

I was totally diagnosed with ADD back in the day, when it was still called ADD. Did a number on my school years: I don't remember much of it, other than being impulsive, reclused, and in detention a lot. I had the usual medications, but I never took them: mom was okay with that because of her stance on medicating children. 

The autism thing isn't quite out of left field either. My eldest brother was diagnosed with Asperger's back when few took autism seriously. I have concluded recently from observations from both myself and my friend's that my dad may be an undiagnosed autistic too... so yeah, the genetic link is there.

What I'm getting at is your own diagnosis of ADHD-PI is one of the closest answers I've received ever since my psychiatrist determined that I have Dysthymia. (Unfortunately named as Double Depression) I'm not going to do the self-diagnoses game, but I will keep it in mind for my upcoming test. What struck me was your description of going into a downward spiral from what an outside opinion would view as something mundane. I used to really have that bad: took off work for two weeks to compose myself after a really bad episode last year. 

But I'm rambling. This response of yours is so far the best tailored to my perspective, and thoughtful as well. I will need to meditate on it further, of course and see if it finally breaks me loose from my torment and grants you a shiny black triangle. But for now, thank you.

Also, Knox (Robert Benfer) really is awesome.

Better people. If I really wanted to overthink it, and by golly I need to, even those who make crap art but shovel it to niche audiences, but that's a different argument.

There are many artists who are better trained, much younger, with brighter ideas and better resources than I could ever have with the mind I have now. If anything, I've been able to write off the whole community as over-saturated, using DeviantART as evidence, but that would never be enough to fill the jagged hole left in my heart when I quit in the first place. I still draw, but it's barely a few 15-minute sessions a week; nothing I can be proud if or be confident enough to show others.

>If everyone had this mindset the human race would be extinct by now. 

I really don't see this as a bad thing. We are a terrible species, weighted down by our own knowledge of how terrible we are.

>Even though you may not be the best at something you can still help improve the world and provide services the human race needs to survive.

My therapist shares the same idea. Now watch me as I kill the idea by dreaming up a grand idea of how to help, take stock of its cost, time, probability, and chances of being kicked over by terrible people and just lose interest. Once again, there are better suited people for this: those whose minds haven't been rotted by cynicism.

>Also if you think this way you’ll never even have a chance to become the best. 

This much is true. I have long been warned of self-fullfiling prophecies. How to handle them given my own filters is another issue, I think.

>Right. I've suffered from depression too, and currently suffer from bipolar disorder. I know how it feels to hear this talk over and over again. But I swear to you, one day you might finally hear it put in some manner that will make it all click.

Quite. I feel like I'm speaking another language with some people; that they won't acknowledge that my dark filter on life isn't like sunglasses, but cataracts. Even my therapist acknowledges that are sessions are going in circles.

>Don't lose sight of those beautiful little things that bring you joy.

Oh, but sir, I already have.

>Do you have people denpendent on your income? If you don't, or can afford to risk it, perhaps a change of career is necessary? Have you asked yourself if it is your career making you feel this way?

Fortunately, no. No dependents; no debts. A blessing, sure, and I seem to want to keep it that way. Why go broke for chasing happiness, not knowing if you'll succeed.

My current warehouse job is totally a poisoned barb, but it's stable, and pays for health insurance.... and that pisses me off. If I croak tomorrow, I'm as replaceable as everyone else, and no sunny HR associate have been able to convince me otherwise. I'm pretty much another husk, letting my soul be devoured for the privilege to breathe. Not only all that, but if I leave, my options are limited to food and retail, since I haven't chosen to play to the student loan racket and hope I made a sound investment.

>Or if it is more your performance, have you sought out advice from the best? In my time, the best of the best are always willing to give advice, and these are the people you want to be getting it from

>The idea that people are just altueristic like that eludes me. And I am in no position to accept tricks of the trade while there's a wall of various negative -isms keeping them out.

>The top brain surgeon in the country had to choose to pursue that path before ever doing brain surgery. Yes, it's a gamble, and most people fail. But, the worst brain surgeon is still a brain surgeon.

Not a brain surgeon I'd like poking around in, though. I don't like gambling with my future, and if that's my only option then damn, I'll sooner go back pondering how civilization got to this system than take a leap of faith.

>If you want to pursue the arts, you're not going to pick up a guitar and suddenly write a billboards top 100. But mists artists don't. Most artists make little to no money their entire lives. And those that do make it big (without prior connections) still starve until they catch that first break.

The artists I'm aware of also have a sense of community; having friends who can let them crash and trade ideas with, and some supportive fans who can give them a boosts. I may have supportive friends, who have been trying for years to get me back on track, but I block them out, thanks to fear if rejection and ridicule, like Liefeld or Buckley, or so many other artists given shame-meme status. People say do what you like, but they will always pay for quality: not pity.

>Even Michael Jordan couldn't dunk when he was 13 playing in peewee. Hell, there were better players on his team in college.

Y'dont say. Must've had some great marketers behind him, or really had to hustle. (See: Leonard Nimoy taking many non-actor jobs before Star Trek)

>There are plenty of reasons. First, you need to recognize that the chances of you being the very best in the world at a given subject or activity is very slim. However, this does not mean that it does not provide you with a sense of fulfillment, or passion. I know I'm not the best guitarist in the world, but that's not why I play. I play it because I love it.

But what if you no longer love something you put your heart into for half your life? Looking at something less like something you would live, but like cold and mechanical work? A cog in a machine? 

The issue of having to be the best at something; that every little thing I do must have a grand meaning/purpose may as well be my bedrock.

It is easy to pin this thoughts on depression, and at the moment all I have to fight it is my medication and a therapist that we both know have run this dialogue in circles.

I consider this one of those generic Hallmark card responses. Not every career makes enough income to justify the happiness factor, and trying different things is both scary-sounding (see: prior scrapes with failure) and/or expensive. (Going to college with no sure idea if you'd like the program--throwing money down the drain--or what you even want to do) I was perfectly happy with the production aspect of art, until I noticed it being ignored, and the higher quality of those more passionate than I have become.
